# A type-erased field whose type a sibling tag selects is one tagged enum with its tag

Status: `open`: the change is crustify `755ff2c` on
`libgit2-crustify/evolution/type-erased-field-tagged-by-a-sibling`, awaiting its review.

## Signal

I had to work out a rule by hand that a skill should have stated.

## Evidence

`wave-186/batch-2/run-1` wrapped `src/cli/opt.h`'s `cli_opt_spec`, whose `void *value`
points at an `int` for a spec of type `CLI_OPT_TYPE_BOOL`, `_SWITCH` or `_ACCUMULATOR`, at a
`char *` for `_VALUE` and `_ARG`, at a `char **` for `_ARGS`, and at nothing for `_NONE` and
`_LITERAL`: `opt.c`'s `parse_long`, `parse_short` and `parse_arg` cast it by the spec's `type`
before they write through it. `binding-types`' Field accessors section gives a type-erased
field "a generic element type when it is known, and the discovered untyped lifetime strategy
otherwise". Neither fits: the type is known, but per object, from a sibling field. Separate
setters for `type` and `value` would let safe code store an `int *` and then retype the spec
as `_VALUE`, so that the next read hands out a `Cell<Option<Arg>>` over an `int`. That is UB
reached from safe code, held by data the native code can change, against `binding`'s Safe
boundary.

The batch bound the pair as the Unions section binds a union and its discriminator. One
`Target<'p>` enum has a variant per kind, each holding its variable's safe form
(`&'p Cell<c_int>`, `&'p Cell<Option<Arg<'p>>>`, `&'p ArgsSlot<'p>`). `SpecRef::target` reads
both fields, and `SpecMut::set_target` writes both. `SpecRef::kind` reads the tag alone, and
nothing writes it alone (`src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`, anchors `fld::cli_opt_spec.value` and
`fld::cli_opt_spec.type` on both accessors).

## Destination

The spec: `binding-types`' Field accessors section, which the binder evolves.

## Change

crustify `755ff2c`. The type-erased bullet of the Field accessors section gains one
sentence. A field whose pointee's type a sibling field selects, as a kind tag does, is
presented as a union is: one tagged enum over the tag and the pointer, each variant holding
its type's safe form, read from both and written together, so that no setter writes the tag
alone. The change drafts its `EVOLUTION.md` entry.

## Record

The row for `EVOLUTION.md`, copied in when the change lands. The change was made as crustify
`755ff2c`, which also edited `EVOLUTION.md`; on 2026-11-14 it was put on the working branch's
tip as `7b738b9`, the same diff without that edit, since a change's row is drafted in its
proposal. It sits on crustify `166d8fd`, and its review reads `7b738b9`.

| change | from | landed as | signal answered | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| a type-erased field whose type a sibling tag selects is one tagged enum with its tag | `libgit2-crustify`, `type-erased-field-tagged-by-a-sibling` | crustify `7b738b9` | `binding-types` had a type-erased field take one element type or the untyped strategy, and left a `void *` whose pointee a sibling kind field selects to be worked out by hand | a binding of such a field with a setter that writes its tag or its pointer alone, or a review finding of its pointer read as the wrong type after a tag write | watched |

## Validation

No failure prompted the change, and this batch's `Spec` is the case. Its `unit_pub` tests
round-trip every variant and check that a retyping write replaces the variable with the kind
(`targets_round_trip_with_their_kinds`, `set_target_replaces_kind_and_variable`). Its
`equiv` test has C's `cli_opt_parser_next` write each kind's variable through a table built
with `set_target` (`c_parses_a_table_built_in_rust`). Both pass on plain and under
ASan+UBSan, and the Rust-only ones under Miri.

content.content:
---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

A lesson is not filed as a proposal: `LESSONS.md` records it. A defect in a tool found
while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

## 5. Lessons

The campaign's lessons sit in `crustify/LESSONS.md`, read by every run of the campaign
before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

A lesson steers every later run, as a rule of the spec does, so it is reviewed:

- A new or changed lesson is `provisional`. The first review batch whose worklist holds the
  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

The lessons are reconciled at each ship point, and whenever five have been added or changed
since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

## 6. Changes

A campaign evolves each component, Crustify or a tool, on a working branch of its own in
that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

A change is made on a branch named `<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>`, forked from that
working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a
fast-forward, the worktree is purged and the branch deleted. Its commits take the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives the
campaign's.

- A change to the spec follows `authoring`: written once, in the place its kind belongs,
  as generally as the evidence allows.
- A change to what a tool does comes with a regression test: the reproducer of a defect
  becomes one, and a new behaviour gets one that fails without it. A change to its
  documentation alone adds none, unless the defect it fixes has a reproducer, which becomes

  against a build installed as a dependent installs it. The tool's whole suite passes, its
  opt-in tests included wherever the change touches what they cover.

  subcommand of an existing tool within that tool's goals, or as a script in the skill
  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is
  merged upstream only with the user's approval.

landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

## 7. Validation

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

A spec change that a failure prompted is validated by running again what failed, the item,
the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

one that made it. A change is finished once its proposal names its commit. A finished
change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on
the fix rather than around it. The review reads the proposal, the change and its validation, and checks

- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;

- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;

record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads

|---|---|

| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`

put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

would hold for any C codebase.

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section

## 11. The record

# Authoring

How Crustify is organized: its skills, its agents and the providers that serve them to an
agent host, and where each kind of text lives. The aim is that every rule is written once,
in the one place its kind belongs, so that changing it changes every agent that follows it,
and no two copies drift apart.

## 1. Layers

Crustify is text in three layers, with one more per run:

| layer | where | voice | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| skills | `skills/<group>/<name>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what Crustify's artifacts are and how its work is done: workflows, how-tos, conventions, schemas |
| tool skills | `skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what each tool is, and how it serves each stage |
| agents | `agents/<agent>.md`, with `agents/common.md`, and the assistant's under `agents/assistant/` | instructive, second person | an agent's identity, inputs, what it owns, its steps and what its role changes in the skill index |
| task messages | `task.md` beside a run's `task.json` | instructive | what one run is given: its inputs, and what it needs beyond its role |

Each artifact's schema, the meaning of its fields, is a skill under `skills/artifacts/`,
and an example of each is given under `templates/`, which the schema cites. The settings,
dashboard and `.gitignore` templates there are what a campaign copies to start. Examples
hold illustrations, not rules.

The layers are plain Markdown, so that any agent reads them as files. A provider, under
`providers/<host>/`, serves them to one agent host in its own format, as
[Providers](#4-providers) describes; the layers name no host.

### 1.1 Skills

A skill describes. It states what an artifact holds, how a decision is made, what a
procedure produces and when each of its steps happens, never what an agent should do, and
never who does a step: which agent owns which step is the agents'. It does not name the
tools that serve it either: a skill reads the same whether or not a tool is installed, so
a statement such as "each unit's lifecycle role is established while planning" belongs in
a skill, and the wavefront command that records it belongs in wavefront's tool skill.

Skills are grouped by the part of the work they describe: `workflows/`, `planning/`,
`rust/`, `verification/`, `operations/`, `artifacts/`, `tools/` and `crustify/`. A skill's
name is unique across the groups, since agents invoke it by name. Two kinds of skill
describe how work is done. A how-to, such as `binding` or `porting`, describes how one item
is handled. A workflow, under `workflows/`, describes how one kind of campaign proceeds
from its settings to its results: `setup`, which every campaign shares, and one per kind of
campaign (`binding-workflow`, `porting-workflow`, `audit-workflow`). A workflow names the
how-tos and the layout rather than restating them.

A skill opens with frontmatter that gives its `name` and its `description`. The
description is all an agent sees of the skill before it reads it, so it says what the skill
covers and before which step it is read. A skill stays under about 4,500 tokens, so that a
host that brings an invoked skill back after compacting an agent's context brings it back
whole; one that outgrows that is split at a section that another step needs on its own.
The parts sit in sub-directories of the skill's own, `skills/<group>/<skill>/<part>/SKILL.md`,
each named `<skill>-<part>`, and the skill's own `SKILL.md` keeps what they share: `binding`
and `porting` keep their boundaries, and their `-types` and `-symbols` parts their routes.

A skill's directory may also hold a script the skill describes, with its tests beside it,
standard library only, so that it runs wherever the skill is read: `usage` holds
`crustify-usage`.

A skill or an agent says what a step does and which program does it, never the program's
command lines, flags or options, which change with the program: the program's own `--help`
and documentation give them, and the text sends its reader there. A command appears only
where its exact form is what must hold, and a procedure of several commands that must run
exactly so is a script beside its skill, documented by its own `--help`.

Every skill's sections are numbered. A reference to a section names it, with or without its
number ("testing-builds' Coverage section", "layout § Lifecycle › Waves"), so that a renumbering
never silently points a reference at another section. A skill links another by its
relative path, with the other's name as the link's text.

### 1.2 Agents

An agent instructs. Its file holds what is specific to it: its place among the agents, its
inputs, its workflow steps, and the guidelines that apply to one step or stage. Where a step
follows a skill, the agent names the skill's section rather than restating it ("as the
`scheduling` skill's Order section describes"); where a step adds to it, the agent states
only the addition.

An agent states what it owns by naming the skill sections it carries out ("you create and
purge every level of the `layout` skill's Lifecycle section"), and adds only what the
skills leave to it: the commands it runs, the judgements it makes, the cases it must not
handle itself.

Every agent's prompt opens with `agents/common.md`: that every commit takes the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives, that a task
message's instructions take precedence over the rest of the prompt, except where a skill or a
role says a task message adds to a check and never relaxes it, and how skills and
tool skills are read. Every agent sees every skill, with its description:
its host lists them, or, for a host that does not, the provider fills the index of every
skill at common's `<!-- SKILL INDEX -->` marker from the skills' names and descriptions, so
that each description is written once.

The agent's own file follows, in three sections, every agent alike:

- `## Role`: who the agent is, its place among the agents, what it owns and what it leaves
  to others;
- `## Workflow`: its steps, each naming the skills it follows. A skill the description
  already sends the agent to before a step needs no mention; a step names a skill where
  only part of it applies to the agent, or where the agent follows it only in some runs;
  and
- `## Inputs`: what its task message names.

An agent's file names no value of one run: an integration branch or a batch id is "the one
your task message names". `{crustify_root}` stands for the path of Crustify's checkout,
which a provider fills.

The assistant has one file for every kind of campaign, `agents/assistant/assistant.md`, with a
`<!-- CAMPAIGN ROLE -->` marker at the end of its Role and a `<!-- CAMPAIGN WORKFLOW -->`
marker as its Workflow, which take the campaign kind's file,
`agents/assistant/translate.md` for a port or wrap campaign or `agents/assistant/audit.md`
for an audit: its `### Campaign` section, what the assistant owns in that kind of campaign,
and, after its `<!-- WORKFLOW -->` marker, its steps.

### 1.3 Tool skills

A tool is one program an agent reaches for: wavefront, ffimap, ffibox. Each has one skill,
`skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md`, written as every skill is, descriptively and without naming
agents. It states what a campaign uses the tool for, where the tool's state sits in a
campaign, and how the tool's output becomes Crustify's artifacts and decisions. How the
tool works, its configuration, tables, commands and what they mean, is its own
documentation's, which the skill cites by document rather than restating, so that the two
never drift; a fact that documentation lacks is added to it, on a branch of the tool's
repository, not to the skill.

A tool skill opens with what the tool is, which documentation of its own is read in full
before its first use, and what holds in every use of it; one section per stage follows,
each subsection named after the skill section it adds to ("Scheduling › Order"), stating
only what the tool adds there and naming the documents of the tool that stage reads. Its
description names the stages and steps it serves.

An agent reads a tool's skill before the first step of its work that the skill's
description names, as `agents/common.md` says, and no other skill names a tool: the
description alone brings an agent to the tool, so it names every stage and step the tool
serves. A tool is removed by deleting its skill.

## 2. Placement

| text | goes in |
|---|---|
| what an artifact's fields mean | its schema skill under `skills/artifacts/` |
| what an artifact looks like | its example under `templates/` |
| how a kind of work is done, independent of tools | the skill for that work |
| how a kind of campaign proceeds, step by step | its workflow skill under `skills/workflows/`, with the steps every campaign shares in `setup` |
| a convention every agent follows | `conventions` |
| what one agent does, in which steps, and which steps it owns | that agent's file under `agents/` |
| what every agent holds | `agents/common.md` |
| what the assistant does in one kind of campaign | `agents/assistant/<kind>.md` |
| what a tool is, and how it serves each stage | its tool skill |
| how one host is served the layers | its provider under `providers/<host>/` |
| what one run needs beyond its role | its task message, `task.md` |
| what Crustify is for, which every change is judged against | `GOALS.md`, at Crustify's root |
| how Crustify repairs and improves itself | [`evolution`](../evolution/SKILL.md) |
| which changes landed, and whether each held | `EVOLUTION.md`, at Crustify's root |
| a rule that holds for one target alone | that campaign's `crustify/LESSONS.md` |

A rule that two agents share goes in a skill both read, not in both agents. A rule that
names a tool goes in the tool's skill. A change to a rule is made where the rule lives;
text that restates it elsewhere is removed rather than kept in step.

## 3. Runs

A stage's agent runs with its file as its system prompt and its task as its first message:
the task message names what its `## Inputs` section lists and the instructions its run
needs beyond its role, if any. Its file is the same for every run of the stage, so that runs at once share their
whole system prompt in the provider's cache. The assistant runs the same way, as the main
agent of a session in a campaign's repository, with its file and its campaign kind's as
its system prompt.

## 4. Providers

A provider serves the layers to one agent host, in that host's format, and holds nothing
the layers do not: every file it carries is generated from them, wires them in, or carries
what its host needs of its own.

The generic provider, `providers/generic/`, composes each agent's prompt for any host:
`compose.py <agent> [<kind>]` prints `agents/common.md`, with the skill index filled, and
the agent's file, the assistant's with its campaign kind's. A host without a provider of
its own takes that prompt as its agent's instructions, and reads each skill's `SKILL.md`
by its path. The other providers compose through it.

The Claude Code provider, `providers/claude/`, makes Crustify's checkout a plugin, whose
manifest is `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:

- the skills, by their group directories and the directory of each part of a split skill,
  which the manifest lists on its own since Claude Code scans a listed directory one level
  deep, invoked as `crustify:<name>`;
- `agents/`, one plugin agent per stage, `crustify:<stage>`, and one assistant per campaign
  kind, `crustify:assistant-translate` and `crustify:assistant-audit`. A plugin agent's
  body replaces Claude Code's own system prompt, so each body opens with that prompt,
  `system-prompt.md`, followed by the generic provider's prompt without the skill index,
  since Claude Code lists the plugin's skills to every agent. Each agent's
  frontmatter gives the description the assistant routes a run by;
- `system-prompt.md`, Claude Code's own system prompt, captured from a real request by
  `dump-system-prompt.py`, less its one project's `# Memory` section, and dumped again
  when Claude Code is upgraded;
- `spawn.py`, which launches a stage run as a Claude Code process of its own, since Claude
  Code refuses a subagent's writes of report files, and copies its transcript into
  Crustify's home; the assistants' prompts end with how they launch through it;
- `hooks.json`: a `SubagentStop` hook, `transcripts.py`, which copies each stage agent's
  transcript into Crustify's home, for a stage run a host launches as a subagent; and
- `compose.py`, which generates the agents (`compose.py build`).

The generated files are committed, and regenerated whenever `agents/` or
`system-prompt.md` changes.

## 5. Language

Programmers and agents read Crustify's texts and a campaign's, so they are written plainly,
as the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style)
describes: one term per thing, short sentences, a condition before its consequence, lists for
parallel items. A rule keeps its reason, since agents generalize from reasons. A rewrite keeps
every fact of the old text, which its review checks. The voice rules of [Layers](#1-layers)
stay: a skill describes, an agent instructs.

---
name: binding-types
description: "How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding, binding's type route: its surface, safe layout, lifecycle and field accessors, unions as tagged enums, enums and typedefs. Read before binding any type, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Binding types

How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding: the type route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section; the symbols it reaches are
[`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s. [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)
starts from it.

## 1. Surface

A binding's surface is the fields and lifecycle primitives the public API publishes: in a
wrap batch that precedes its consumers, the fields those consumers access and the
type's lifecycle primitives, so that a type none of whose fields they access is bound
opaque.
Releasers, field disposers, cloners, constructors, casts and pointer-field semantics are
identified before a representation is chosen.

## 2. Safe layout

A type is bound as a safe layout over the raw type and its handles. The canonical wrapped
surface has three types, named as the conventions describe:

| type | role |
|---|---|
| `Foo` | layout-compatible newtype named in every owner and handle, and held by value only in Rust-owned storage (a local, or embedded) |
| `FooRef<'a>` | copyable shared borrowed handle with getters |
| `FooMut<'a>` | exclusive borrowed handle with setters, and shared and exclusive reborrows |

Its owners, which [Lifecycle](#3-lifecycle) describes, are named `FooBox` and `FooArc`, as
the conventions name them too. These names are what consumers use, whatever they name: here

offers: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the

such as an owner's raw access, is no part of the safe API.

No Rust reference to the wrapped C object is ever formed. Borrowed handles contain
pointers and carry lifetimes; references to handles cover Rust-owned handle storage only.

unsafe blocks.

A synthetic type generator is bound as:

- a generic wrapper for a homogeneous family converging on the generator;
- an alias of a dominant concrete instance to the generator with its element wrapper; and
- specializations only for behaviour that differs from the generic surface.

## 3. Lifecycle

Every ownership variant the analysis supports has a representation.

Owners never dereference to `Foo`; they hand out handles. A sole owner, or a `Foo` value,
produces `FooRef` and `FooMut` through `as_ref()` and `as_mut()`. A shared owner without a
lock produces `FooRef` directly, and `FooMut` only when it can prove its reference is the
only one, or after copying the object. A shared owner whose object carries its own lock
produces both through read and write guards, which hold the lock while the handle lives.

Lifecycle and clone
strategies are stateless, layout-compatible and statically selected when the state is
recoverable from the object; runtime state is carried only when construction, destruction
or cloning needs external data.

possible it is exported as a safe function returning the fully-formed object. Every type an
argument names is wrapped before it, since a wrap brings in its signature's types.

C lifecycle primitives are kept while C can allocate or free the storage.

A type whose address C keeps beyond the call that receives it, to read it, call back with it
or free it, as the analysis establishes, is never moved while C keeps it: a value of it
held by value is never handed to C to keep, and an owner that could move it out is
pinned.

Promoting construction-phase storage into an owner is unsafe, so it is encapsulated in the
type's safe constructor: consumers of the public API never call `assume_init` in their own
unsafe blocks.

Lifecycle routines are also scheduled as free symbols, although the type route emits them
as it binds their types; the symbol route, [`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s,
skips those a type batch already emitted.

## 4. Field accessors

Each accessor follows from the ownership, mutability, nullability, cardinality and lifetime
findings, and every pointer-derived result is tied to the state that keeps it alive.

Getters that read `Foo`'s fields are methods in `impl FooRef` blocks taking `&self`, and
setters that write them are methods in `impl FooMut` blocks taking `&mut self`. A field is
read through the shared handle's pointer and written through the mutable handle's pointer,
projected with `addr_of!`, `addr_of_mut!`, `&raw const` or `&raw mut`, never with

- An owned-reference field has a replacement setter that drops the old owner, an owning
  getter that leaves the field valid, and a shared borrowed getter.
- A by-value wrapped field has a shared or mutable handle over the projected place.
- A stored borrow without an expressible lifetime has an unsafe setter whose caller
  contract carries the referent-lifetime obligation.

  trait where useful.
- A runtime ownership flag has separately checked owned and borrowed operations.

  [Unions](#5-unions) describes.
- Scalar and array variants have separate typed forms.
- A type-erased field takes a generic element type when it is known, and the discovered
  untyped lifetime strategy otherwise.

  proof.

and strings, arrays and erased owners through real release strategies.

emitted with the type.

## 5. Unions

A union is not bound as a type of its own: the types its members hold are bound, and the
union is presented where it is used, a field accessor or a function's signature, as a
tagged Rust enum, with a variant for each member, each over its member's safe type. One
tagged enum stands in for the union at every use. Its tag is the discriminator the
analysis establishes as selecting the active member: a sibling field, a parameter, or a
predicate over sibling fields, such as a length that is zero only while an inline member
is active. Reading the union evaluates the discriminator to choose the variant, and
writing it writes both.

A union whose active member nothing beside it selects, its tag held by what refers to it,
such as the sign of the index that reaches it, is presented by an `unsafe` accessor for
each member, whose caller contract states which member must be active.

## 6. Enums

An enum is bound to a safe Rust type over the constants bindgen generates for it:

- a closed enum is a Rust enum, with a variant for each of its constants;
- an enum whose constants C combines as flags is a `#[repr(transparent)]` newtype over its
  integer type, with an associated constant for each of its constants and the bitwise
  operators, since a combination is no variant; and
- an enum without a name has no type to bind: its constants become constants of its
  integer type.

Beneath a closed enum's safe type sits its integer form, the interop layer C needs: a
`#[repr]` over the enum's integer type, as bindgen gives it, each constant's value its
variant's discriminant, and the conversions through which its values cross the boundary
as that integer. A value from C is converted fallibly where it enters Rust, since C may
pass one the enum does not name, which a Rust enum may not hold: such a value takes the
path the C gives an invalid value, or an error of the safe API where it gives none. A
binding keeps the integer form for good, since C implements what produces and consumes
the enum's values.

## 7. Typedefs

A typedef of its own, one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer, gives
another name to a type that has a Rust form already: a primitive, an array, a pointer, or a
type another link unit or an out-of-tree library's wrapper owns. It is bound under its own
name to the Rust form the analysis shapes from its uses: an alias of the type it names where
they give it no meaning that type lacks, and a type of its own where they do, an invariant,
an ownership or a type erasure that an alias would flatten. Its raw form is no part of the
safe API, as [`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section describes, and it has no interop layer of
its own: its values cross the boundary as those of the type it names do.

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the

route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the

the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

# Goals

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 1. Safety

No undefined behaviour is reachable from safe Rust. The unsafe code that remains sits in its
regions, and is sound for every input.

### The unsafe surface

- **Measure.** What a deterministic scan counts on each landing:
  - raw pointers and `unsafe fn`s on the public API;
  - unsafe lines and raw dereferences; and
  - unsafe code outside its regions.

  The first two fall as a module goes from wrapped to ported and through its later stages.
  The third is zero throughout.
- **Paired with** soundness, below. Calling an unsound function safe takes an obligation off
  the API, and so lowers this measure.

### Soundness

- **Measure.** The defects a reproducer proves, as the review reports file them by kind.
  These defects are undefined behaviour and contracts that can be broken.
- **Paired with** the escapes among these defects.
- **Not taken yet.** The tier that caught a defect. Also the unsafe sites a review read,
  which the defects are counted against.

## 2. Equivalence

The Rust keeps the C's specified behaviour, not its bugs. The specified behaviour is what
the C's documentation, tests and consumers rely on.

- **Measure.**
  - The target's own tests passing over the Rust at each switch, against their recorded
    baseline.
  - The inputs and states on which the Rust is compared with the C it replaces, with no
    difference left unexplained.
  - The differences made on purpose, each documented and held by a test.
- **Paired with** the differences found after the comparison ended. They are found by a
  review, at a switch, or by a consumer.
- **Not taken yet.** The inputs compared and the deliberate differences, as figures. Each
  run's notes alone hold them.

## 3. Idiomatic Rust

The API a Rust consumer sees is native Rust: ownership, borrowing, errors, iteration and
traits. It is not C's conventions behind a Rust syntax.

- **Measure.** The C forms that Safety's scan still counts on the public API: raw and
  untyped pointers, and obligations handed to callers. Also the ergonomics and idiom
  findings that reviews file, counted per item reviewed.
- **Paired with** the ergonomics and idiom findings that a later tier or a consumer makes on
  an item an earlier review passed. A review that reads less finds less.
- **Not taken yet.** Which tier made a finding.

## 4. Performance

The emitted Rust costs no more than native Rust would. Where tokens and time buy
accuracy, the harness spends them.

### The harness

- **Measure.** Cost and wall time per translated item, reviews and switches included.
- **Paired with** what was redone: batches run again, gates rerun and merges made twice.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures: cheaper work with more escapes is not
  cheaper.

### The emitted Rust

- **Measure.** The emitted Rust's time and memory against the C it replaces, on the target's
  own workloads.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures, since a check dropped is time saved.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.
  <!-- TODO: no campaign benchmarks what it ports; which workloads, and at which event,
  is not specified. -->

# Goals

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 1. Safety

No undefined behaviour is reachable from safe Rust. The unsafe code that remains sits in its
regions, and is sound for every input.

### The unsafe surface

- **Measure.** What a deterministic scan counts on each landing:
  - raw pointers and `unsafe fn`s on the public API;
  - unsafe lines and raw dereferences; and
  - unsafe code outside its regions.

  The first two fall as a module goes from wrapped to ported and through its later stages.
  The third is zero throughout.
- **Paired with** soundness, below. Calling an unsound function safe takes an obligation off
  the API, and so lowers this measure.

### Soundness

- **Measure.** The defects a reproducer proves, as the review reports file them by kind.
  These defects are undefined behaviour and contracts that can be broken.
- **Paired with** the escapes among these defects.
- **Not taken yet.** The tier that caught a defect. Also the unsafe sites a review read,
  which the defects are counted against.

## 2. Equivalence

The Rust keeps the C's specified behaviour, not its bugs. The specified behaviour is what
the C's documentation, tests and consumers rely on.

- **Measure.**
  - The target's own tests passing over the Rust at each switch, against their recorded
    baseline.
  - The inputs and states on which the Rust is compared with the C it replaces, with no
    difference left unexplained.
  - The differences made on purpose, each documented and held by a test.
- **Paired with** the differences found after the comparison ended. They are found by a
  review, at a switch, or by a consumer.

name: evolution-record
description: "The record of the changes that landed in Crustify and its tools, `EVOLUTION.md`: its rows, their recurrence signals and statuses, when the watched rows are read, and how evolution itself evolves from the record. Read before drafting a change's row, writing or reading the record, or proposing a change to the evolution protocol."
---

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep

description: "The record of the changes that landed in Crustify and its tools, `EVOLUTION.md`: its rows, their recurrence signals and statuses, when the watched rows are read, and how evolution itself evolves from the record. Read before drafting a change's row, writing or reading the record, or proposing a change to the evolution protocol."

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.

## Evolution

14. **How far may the campaign evolve Crustify and its tools from what it exposes? Agents
    file proposals and record the target's lessons; fixes and improvements land, once
    another agent has reviewed them, on a working branch of each component that is the
    campaign's own, and reach the component's `devel` only with your approval.**
    (`id: evolution`)
    - Answer: `evolve`, on the campaign's working branches (`libgit2-crustify/devel` of each
      component, which the campaign's checkouts are on since 2026-11-12): a change lands
      there once its review approves it, and each component's `devel` takes the working
      branch only with the user's approval, as crustify `c2f21a0`'s model has it. The
      former `unattended: the whole campaign` is retired with it.
    - `propose`: proposals and lessons only. `repair`: also fixes of defects. `evolve`: also
      improvements and new tools. You are asked to take the working branches into `devel`
      at each module's end and the campaign's end.

content.content:
### Scheduling › Order

The link units and modules are ordered from the configuration, after its T3 tables are
written, and reviewed there:

- every type-erased parameter and field with no cast, followed until it is read as a named
  type, stored, returned or lost. A hop that dispatches on a tag and reads different types
  per branch establishes none of them;
- every cast edge wavefront derives between two public types, each that is no type
  relation dropped;
- every public type in a cast relation, the pairs that are a hierarchy recorded as
  `base_derived` rows; and
- the type-minting macros, the source checked for invocations that conditional

### Analysis

An item's analysis queries the campaign's configuration, and its findings are submitted
to the ownership store. A type-erased parameter or field is looked up in the T3 tables before it
is bound, and the binding names the type a row gives it rather than a raw pointer. The
instances of a type generator share one generic, with per-instance aliases.

### Binding types › Surface

A type's lifecycle primitives are identified as `docs/type-lifecycle.md` describes, and
their `Pin`, unchanged for its consumers.

## 2. Unions

A union's safe API is the tagged Rust enum [`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Unions
section presents it as, from its port. Its storage keeps the C union, with its
discriminator beside it, while C uses its layout, and is ported as a struct's is, with the
same later stages: its `port/layout` makes the tagged enum its storage, the discriminator
folded into the enum's tag. A union whose tag what refers to it holds becomes a tagged
enum too, once no other C uses its layout, its referrers' tags folded into it.

## 3. Enums

A ported enum takes the safe type [`binding-types`](../../binding/types/SKILL.md)'s Enums section gives
it, and its header keeps the C definition for the remaining C: the two are not linked,

## 11. Consistency

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

- **Measure.** The conventions findings reviews file, per item.
- **Paired with** two measures, since a review that reads less finds less:
  - the items a later batch or review reshaped; and
  - the conventions findings a later tier makes on an item an earlier review passed.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - both paired measures;
  - the departures that state their reason, against the departures a review had to find; and
  - whether an item translated twice took the same shape both times.

## 12. Attribution

# Builds in this repository run the raw bindings in campaign mode, against the `plain`
# variant unless CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT names another, or is set empty to build as a
# dependent would (crustify's `bindgen` skill, Build modes).
[env]
CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT = "plain"
# pcre2-sys links the PCRE2 that pkg-config finds, else builds its vendored copy, which would
# shadow the side campaign's for libgit2's C too: point it at the variant's install
# (crustify/evolution/bundled-pcre2-shadows-the-side-campaign). cargo-variant.sh sets
# another variant's, which this does not override. The install is reached as the variant's
# build found it, from crustify/builds/plain, which a worktree or a gate snapshot links to the
# repository's own: the kernel resolves the `..` past that link, so that every checkout
# reaches the clone beside the repository holding the builds.
PKG_CONFIG_PATH = { value = "crustify/builds/plain/../../../../pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install/lib/pkgconfig", relative = true }

# days, so that an update never takes a release before the ecosystem has seen it. The
# committed Cargo.lock is unaffected; it applies to resolution only.
[registry]
global-min-publish-age = "3 days"

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 8. Incremental migration without breaking consumers

A codebase moves to Rust one module at a time. Every landing builds and passes its gates. No
consumer breaks: a C or Rust consumer's code does not change as what it consumes is wrapped,
ported or moves through its later stages.

- **Measure.**
  - The items whose API changed or went after their first landing, each with its reason.
  - The landed trees that failed a gate.
  - The target's test baseline, which moves only by the cases carried over.
- **Paired with** Idiomatic Rust's measure of C forms on the public API. An API that never
  changes because it stayed C's breaks no one and serves no one.

### The order

- **Measure.** The batches that met a dependency not yet landed, and waited for it, rewrote
  around it or reached past its wrapper.

  Items land after what they depend on. Where the order cuts a cycle, an item lands after
  the binding of what it depends on. That order is how this goal is met, and Safety's and
  Performance's with it: a consumer written once, over a boundary written once.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.

## 9. Generality

The rules hold for any C codebase. What holds for one target alone is that target's lesson,
not a rule.

- **Measure.** Of what a campaign's evidence taught, the share stated as rules without the
  target's names against the share kept as the target's lessons. Also the rules a second
  target could not follow as written.

## 10. Least constraint

A rule states what must hold. Unless the how is itself what must hold, the rule leaves the
how to the agent.

- **Measure.** Per module, the rules that a run:
  - worked around;
  - rewrote sound code to satisfy; or
  - reported as forcing a worse result.
- **Paired with** what a loosened rule let through: the changes marked as weakening a check,
  and the defects found where a rule was loosened.

## 11. Consistency

One kind of item is translated one way. Items that mean the same in C take the same Rust
pattern, whatever their syntax and whichever agent, batch or campaign translates them. The
pattern is the one the conventions and the how-to skills give them. A departure states its
reason.

A pattern a skill gives is a how that must hold, in Least constraint's terms. A pattern is
given only where translating the same thing two ways costs a consumer or a reviewer. Where
the skills give none, the agent chooses. A choice met twice, where two ways would cost, is
proposed as the pattern rather than left to converge.

- **Measure.** The conventions findings reviews file, per item.
- **Paired with** two measures, since a review that reads less finds less:
  - the items a later batch or review reshaped; and
  - the conventions findings a later tier makes on an item an earlier review passed.
- **Not taken yet.**
  - both paired measures;
  - the departures that state their reason, against the departures a review had to find; and
  - whether an item translated twice took the same shape both times.

# Evolution record

The record of what [`evolution`](../SKILL.md) landed, and what evolution learns from it.

## 1. Record

Every change that lands is recorded in Crustify's own repository, in
[`EVOLUTION.md`](../../../../EVOLUTION.md), whatever component it changed, so that a later
campaign can tell whether it held. A row gives the campaign and proposal the change came
from, the component and commit it landed as, the signal it answered, its recurrence signal
and its status, with a change that weakens a check marked so in its status. A change no
proposal filed names its campaign and `no proposal` in its place, with where it came from.
A proposal that lands several changes takes a row for each.

A change's row is drafted in its proposal, so that the review reads it. The record's writer
copies the row into the record when the change lands. An evolution branch never edits
`EVOLUTION.md`, so that two changes awaiting review never conflict there, and the record
has one writer per campaign. The record holds every change landed since it began, on
2026-11-12; what landed before is not recorded.

The recurrence signal is what a campaign would observe if the issue were back, in what a
campaign produces anyway: a review finding of a category, a run that fails for a cause, a
tool's error, a correction the user repeats. A change whose regression test checks all of
it has `test` in its place and is not watched. One with no signal a campaign could observe
has `none`, with why, and is not watched either.

A watched change is:

- `watched` from its landing;
- `recurred` once its signal is met again, with the evidence, which opens a proposal that
  cites the row: the change was wrong or partial, or the validation and review that passed
  it were; and
- `confirmed` once a campaign other than the one it came from has ended, having exercised
  it, without the signal.

A row's signal is looked for at two times, in every campaign:

- when a proposal is indexed, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Proposals section describes:
  a signal that matches a row's recurrence signal marks that row `recurred`; and
- periodically, when the rows still `watched` are read against the findings, failed runs,
  proposals and corrections since the last reading. The campaign sets the period from its
  state, shorter after a change to a check lands or while findings cluster, longer while
  its modules are small: by default, after every fifth module it integrates. The rows are
  always read at each ship point and at an audit's end.

The record is committed on Crustify's working branch of the campaign and reaches `devel`
with it. Rows are appended in landing order and statuses edited in place, so that a merge
of two campaigns' working branches keeps both campaigns' rows, ordered by their landing.
Under `propose`, where no rule changes, the readings still run and their statuses are
committed all the same, since a record commit changes no rule, and they are put to the user
with the campaign's proposals. Under `off`, they do not run.

## 2. Evolving evolution

Evolution evolves from its own record, as everything else does from a campaign's. At a
campaign's end the record and the campaign's proposals are read for what repeats: changes
that recurred; changes the review rejected or the user declined, by cause; signals a run
met that no proposal answered; how long a blocking defect held its run; and what the
reviews bought for what they cost: per change, the findings each round made that held, those
its author's own validation had already caught, the rounds it took and their cost. How deep
a review reads, and how many rounds a kind of change gets, follow from that evidence, not
from a fixed rule. Each is a
signal of this guidance, as [`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Signals section lists them, and its proposal is on this
skill, on the agents' evolution rules or on what the review checks.

Such a proposal is validated and reviewed as any other, and is marked as one that changes
what checks the rest, so that the user reads it on its own before `devel` takes it, as
[`evolution`](../SKILL.md)'s Autonomy section describes.
